function.description: Generates an image based on the provided description and saves it with the specified file name. The image description should be detailed to ensure the resulting image matches the desired subject and surroundings; otherwise, these aspects will be chosen randomly. This function is not intended for generating images from textual data. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

desc.description: A single string that provides a detailed description of the desired image. For example, 'a sunset over the mountains with a lake in the foreground'.

file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

function.description: Converts the provided text content to speech and saves the resulting audio to a file. This function is intended for voice narration and should be used accordingly. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

content.description: The text content that needs to be converted to speech.

content.description: The HTML content to be written to the file. Must contain valid HTML structure.

filename.description: The name of the file to which the HTML content will be written. If not provided, a default filename will be used.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑run example** that shows how you can create a Google Cloud Compute Engine instance that is equipped with an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU and runs Ubuntu 20.04 LTS.

> ⚠️ **Important note** – Google Cloud does **not** currently offer the RTX A6000 GPU.  
> The closest supported GPU family is the **NVIDIA A100** (or the older A5000).  
> If you truly need an RTX A6000 you would have to use a different provider (e.g., AWS, Azure) or wait until Google adds it to their GPU catalog.  
> The example below uses the **NVIDIA A100** GPU, but you can replace it with any other supported GPU type (e.g., `nvidia-tesla-v100`, `nvidia-tesla-p100`, `nvidia-tesla-a5000`) by changing the `guestAccelerator` field.

---

## 1. Prerequisites

| Item | What you need |
|------|---------------|
| **Google Cloud Project ID** | e.g., `my-gcp-project` |
| **Zone** | e.g., `us-central1-a` |
| **Service Account Key** | JSON key file for a service account that has the `roles/compute.admin` role (or equivalent). |
| **gcloud SDK** | Installed and authenticated (`gcloud auth login` or `gcloud auth activate-service-account`). |

---

## 2. Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# Variables
PROJECT_ID="my-gcp-project"
ZONE="us-central1-a"
INSTANCE_NAME="rtx-a6000-ubuntu"
MACHINE_TYPE="n1-standard-8"          # 8 vCPUs, 30 GB RAM
GPU_TYPE="nvidia-tesla-a100"          # Replace with your GPU type
GPU_COUNT=1
IMAGE_FAMILY="ubuntu-2004-lts"
IMAGE_PROJECT="ubuntu-os-cloud"

# Create the instance
gcloud compute instances create "$INSTANCE_NAME" \
  --project="$PROJECT_ID" \
  --zone="$ZONE" \
  --machine-type="$MACHINE_TYPE" \
  --accelerator=type="$GPU_TYPE,count=$GPU_COUNT" \
  --image-family="$IMAGE_FAMILY" \
  --image-project="$IMAGE_PROJECT" \
  --boot-disk-size=200GB \
  --boot-disk-type=pd-ssd \
  --metadata-from-file startup-script=startup.sh \
  --tags=http-server,https-server \
  --scopes=https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform
```

### Explanation of the flags

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--machine-type` | CPU + RAM configuration |
| `--accelerator` | Attach GPU(s) |
| `--image-family` & `--image-project` | Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image |
| `--boot-disk-size` | Size of the boot disk |
| `--boot-disk-type` | SSD for better performance |
| `--metadata-from-file startup-script` | Optional script that runs on first boot (e.g., install NVIDIA drivers) |
| `--tags` | Network tags for firewall rules |
| `--scopes` | OAuth scopes for the instance |

> **Tip:** If you want to automatically install the NVIDIA driver after the instance boots, create a `startup.sh` file with the following content:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
# Install NVIDIA driver
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-470
```

Make sure the file is executable (`chmod +x startup.sh`).

---

## 3. Using the REST API (JSON)

If you prefer to call the Compute Engine REST API directly (e.g., from a script or a custom application), here’s the exact request you would send:

```http
POST https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/instances
Authorization: Bearer {ACCESS_TOKEN}
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-ubuntu",
  "machineType": "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 200,
        "diskType": "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        {
          "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT",
          "name": "External NAT"
        }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorType": "projects/{PROJECT_ID}/zones/{ZONE}/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a100",
      "acceleratorCount": 1
    }
  ],
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": [
        "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"
      ]
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\nsudo apt-get update\nsudo apt-get install -y nvidia-driver-470"
      }
    ]
  },
  "tags": {
    "items": ["http-server", "https-server"]
  }
}
```

### Steps to execute

1. **Obtain an OAuth 2.0 access token** for the Compute Engine scope (`https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform`).  
   You can do this via the `gcloud` CLI:

   ```bash
   ACCESS_TOKEN=$(gcloud auth print-access-token)
   ```

2. **Send the HTTP request** using `curl` or any HTTP client:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST \
     "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/${PROJECT_ID}/zones/${ZONE}/instances" \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer ${ACCESS_TOKEN}" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d @instance.json
   ```

   Where `instance.json` contains the JSON payload above (replace placeholders with actual values).

---

## 4. Quick sanity check

After the instance is created, verify that the GPU is visible:

```bash
# SSH into the instance
gcloud compute ssh rtx-a6000-ubuntu --project="$PROJECT_ID" --zone="$ZONE"

# Inside the instance
nvidia-smi
```

You should see the NVIDIA A100 (or your chosen GPU) listed with its driver version.

---

## 5. Summary

- **gcloud CLI**: Quick, one‑liner, handles authentication automatically.  
- **REST API**: Full control, suitable for programmatic automation.  
- **GPU type**: Replace `nvidia-tesla-a100` with the GPU you actually need (if available).  

Feel free to adapt the machine type, disk size, or network settings to match your workload requirements. Happy computing!
